summaries.example: Imagine a movie made from many still pictures. Each picture lasts only a moment, but the quick stream makes movement seem continuous. Vasubandhu used similar reasoning about people: changing physical and mental events can be linked in a stream without needing a permanent, unchanging self.
summaries.summary: Vasubandhu was an important Buddhist thinker from India, active around the fourth and fifth centuries C.E. His writings explain and criticize many ideas from Buddhist schools, as well as some Hindu traditions. His best-known Abhidharma work argues that there is no permanent self. Instead, a person is a changing stream of physical and mental events connected by causes. This view must still explain memory, responsibility, action, and what happens after death. Vasubandhu also argued that things last only for moments, while connected moments create the appearance of continuity. In later Yogācāra works, he defended “appearance-only”: what we experience as separate objects and selves may be mental appearances rather than independently existing things. He also described three ways to understand an apparent thing: how it appears, the causes that produce its appearance, and its lack of the independent reality we imagine. His biography and the list of works written by him remain disputed among scholars.
key_ideas: Vasubandhu wrote about several Buddhist schools and also argued with non-Buddhist thinkers.
He questioned the idea of a permanent self and explained memory and action through connected causes.
He argued that things that seem solid and lasting may actually be streams of changing events.
In his Yogācāra works, he explored the view that the world we experience is appearance-only.
Scholars disagree about parts of his life story and whether every work linked to him was written by one person.
summaries.why_it_matters: Vasubandhu shows how a philosophical idea can change the way we understand ordinary life. The feeling of being one steady person may be compared with a stream of changing moments. His arguments also ask how memory, kindness, harmful actions, and responsibility can make sense without a permanent soul. Studying him helps us see that Buddhist philosophy included careful debates about mind, reality, language, and cause and effect—not just simple rules or stories.

important_terms.definition: A Buddhist philosopher from India whose writings discuss mind, change, action, and how teachings should be understood.
The Buddhist idea that there is no permanent, separate self hiding behind our changing body, feelings, thoughts, and awareness.
The idea that things last only for very short moments and are replaced by new events connected to them.
A school of Buddhist thought associated with Vasubandhu’s later writings, especially the idea that experience is made of appearances in consciousness.
A made-up idea that helps us group changing parts together, such as calling many changing events “me.”

questions_to_think_about: If everything about us changes, what makes us seem like the same person?
Can a memory exist without an unchanging self?
What is the difference between something real and a useful name for many changing parts?
How might dreams help us think about appearances?

summaries.example: Suppose a person makes a harmful choice today and faces its consequences years later. Vasubandhu does not explain this by saying that an unchanging soul carries a moral stain through time. Instead, he describes a causal sequence: present intentions and actions shape later mental and physical events, which eventually produce results. The word “I” can still be used conventionally, but it refers to a continuing stream rather than to a permanent entity.
summaries.summary: Vasubandhu was a major Indian Buddhist philosopher whose works move among several intellectual traditions. The verses of his Treasury of the Abhidharma summarize Kashmiri Vaibhāṣika positions, while its commentary frequently develops Sautrāntika criticisms. His later works present Yogācāra analyses. This variety makes both his intellectual development and the authorship of the texts attributed to him matters of scholarly dispute; some scholars have even proposed that two historical Vasubandhus were combined in later accounts. A central argument in the Treasury denies that a person is a separate, causally effective entity. What exists are changing aggregates linked in a continuum. Memory, action, and karma are therefore explained by causal succession, not by an enduring self. His theory of momentariness intensifies this view: entities do not remain while acquiring different properties; rather, successive events generate apparent continuity. Vasubandhu also rejects Vaibhāṣika invisible physicality, arguing that moral effects can be explained through intentions, experiences, and transformed dispositions. He attacks a sovereign creator God by arguing that one unchanging cause cannot explain changing, diverse effects without appealing to further causes. In the Twenty Verses and related Yogācāra works, he argues that experienced objects are appearance-only. The three natures distinguish the fabricated appearance, the dependent causal process that produces it, and its perfected emptiness of independent nature. The label “idealist” remains contested because Vasubandhu treats mind and appearances as conventional while reserving ultimate reality for an ineffable suchness.
key_ideas: Vasubandhu’s Commentary on the Treasury of the Abhidharma often presents Vaibhāṣika doctrines in its verses while arguing from a Sautrāntika perspective in the commentary.
His refutation of the self treats the person as a conceptual designation for causally connected aggregates, not as an additional substance.
His account of continuity explains memory, agency, and karmic results through causal series rather than through an enduring soul.
He rejects invisible physicality as an unnecessary entity for explaining the moral effects of bodily and verbal action.
His argument against a creator God claims that a single, unchanging cause cannot adequately explain the world’s diversity and temporal variation.
In Yogācāra texts, he defends appearance-only, analyzes sensory objects through mereological arguments, and explains reality through the three natures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Vasubandhu connects difficult metaphysical questions with practical concerns: how persons persist, how responsibility works, how moral action has consequences, and how perception can mislead us. His work also illustrates a sophisticated form of philosophical interpretation in which scripture is read through context, purpose, and rational consistency rather than always literally. The disputes over his biography, authorship, and classification as an idealist show why historical philosophy requires attention to evidence and competing interpretations.

important_terms.definition: A Buddhist philosopher whose works range across Abhidharma analysis, scriptural interpretation, and Yogācāra metaphysics.
The Abhidharma claim that a permanent self or person cannot be found apart from the changing aggregates.
The view that conditioned entities arise and cease moment by moment rather than persist as substances that change their qualities.
A Buddhist system associated with analyses of consciousness, appearance-only, karmic seeds, and the three natures.
The five changing categories used in Buddhist analysis of a person: physical form, feelings, ideas, dispositions, and consciousness.
Vasubandhu’s distinction between how something appears, the causal process producing that appearance, and the absence of the independent nature attributed to it.
A consciousness described in Yogācāra as preserving karmic seeds and helping explain continuity across experience and rebirth.
A theory that experienced objects lack existence independent of consciousness or mental appearance, at least at the conventional level discussed by Vasubandhu.

questions_to_think_about: Does a causal series provide enough continuity for personal identity and moral responsibility?
Can something be useful in ordinary speech while lacking ultimate independent existence?
Are dreams, hallucinations, or virtual environments good evidence for Vasubandhu’s appearance-only argument?
Does explaining experience through consciousness establish idealism, or only a theory about appearances?
How should philosophical reasoning handle scriptural passages that seem to conflict?

summaries.example: Think about a team project. The team may seem like one thing, but it is really made from different people, conversations, decisions, and changing plans. Vasubandhu’s view of a person is similar: “You” are not a separate permanent object in addition to your body, feelings, thoughts, habits, and awareness. You are a connected process. A promise or mistake can still matter because earlier events help cause later events.
summaries.summary: Vasubandhu was an influential Buddhist philosopher from India, active during the Gupta period. His writings cover Abhidharma philosophy, Buddhist scripture, logic, and Yogācāra thought. He is difficult to classify because he presents several schools and sometimes argues against positions he has just explained. His biography is also uncertain: traditional accounts describe a shift from non-Mahāyāna Buddhist views toward Yogācāra, while some modern scholars see a more gradual development or question whether all the texts belong to one author. In the Treasury of the Abhidharma, Vasubandhu argues against a permanent self. A person is not an extra substance behind the five aggregates; the person is a conventional name for a changing, causally connected stream. This raises problems about memory, agency, and karma, which he answers by describing links between earlier and later events. His momentariness theory says that things do not remain unchanged while their qualities alter. Instead, new events replace earlier ones, creating apparent continuity. He also criticizes special invisible matter used to explain karma and rejects a single creator God as unable to explain a world of changing effects without relying on additional causes. In Yogācāra, he argues that experienced objects are appearance-only. His three-natures account distinguishes what appears, the causes producing the appearance, and the absence of the independent reality we project onto it. Scholars still debate whether “idealist” is the best label, since he treats ordinary mind-based explanations as conventional rather than ultimate.
key_ideas: Vasubandhu wrote from more than one Buddhist viewpoint, so readers must distinguish positions he explains from positions he accepts.
He argued that a permanent self cannot be shown through perception or inference, while changing aggregates can be analyzed.
Continuity does not require an unchanging thing: linked events can explain memory, action, and karmic results.
He criticized the idea of invisible physicality, saying that moral effects can be explained by intentions, experiences, and habits.
He used careful interpretation of Buddhist scriptures, sometimes arguing that a passage has a purpose beyond its most literal reading.
His Yogācāra writings defend appearance-only and describe reality through fabricated, dependent, and perfected natures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Vasubandhu matters because he joins abstract questions to everyday concerns. His philosophy asks what makes a person the same over time, how choices can have later results, and whether perception shows reality exactly as it is. His methods also teach an important reading skill: philosophical and religious texts may require attention to context, purpose, and consistency. The ongoing scholarly disagreements encourage careful judgment instead of accepting a single biography or label too quickly.

important_terms.definition: An Indian Buddhist philosopher whose works compare, organize, and criticize ideas from several Buddhist traditions.
The Buddhist position that no permanent self exists separately from the changing parts of experience.
The doctrine that conditioned things arise and disappear in individual moments, with later moments connected to earlier ones.
A set of Buddhist ideas emphasizing consciousness, mental appearances, and different ways of understanding reality.
The changing physical and mental parts analyzed as making up what we call a person.
An idea or label used to organize many changing events, rather than a separate thing with its own independent existence.
The view that ordinary objects are appearances in consciousness and do not exist independently in the way they seem to.

questions_to_think_about: If a person is a changing process, why do names and responsibilities continue over time?
Can a chain of causes explain freedom and creativity, or does it make choices seem determined?
Why might a teacher use a statement that is not meant to be read literally?
Does the fact that something is an appearance make it unreal or unimportant?
Why might scholars disagree about whether one person wrote all the works attributed to Vasubandhu?
